items.summary: The same prompts for a drowned neo-gothic city shader, less than a year later on GPT-6.2 Astra. This is all procedural (Interestingly, in a very Astra move, the first version it made had deterministic…
items.body:
The same prompts for a drowned neo-gothic city shader, less than a year later on GPT-6.2 Astra. This is all procedural

(Interestingly, in a very Astra move, the first version it made had deterministic elements to make the experience more impressive, no other model has done that) https://t.co/8KUAk9rBuS

quote.text:
Had early access to GPT-5.2. Its an impressive model.

Here is GPT 5.2 Pro's version of "create a visually interesting shader that can run in twigl-dot-app make it like an infinite city of neo-gothic towers partially drowned in a stormy ocean with large waves," single shot.

comments.text: Was it the exact same prompt text both times, word for word? And when the first version added deterministic elements, did a follow-up like "keep everything procedural" fix it in one turn?
comments.text_zh: 两次用的提示词文本是否完全一字不差？而且当第一版加入了确定性元素后，补一句「全部保持程序化生成」是否一轮就能纠正？

comments.text: "It didn't tell me without me asking" is the part I'd watch. A shortcut is fine. An undisclosed one is the problem.
comments.text_zh: “没等我问它就没告诉我”这点我会盯着看。有捷径没关系，隐瞒捷径才是问题。

comments.text: Fits what Artificial Analysis measured today: Astra's answers got shorter and less structured (352→210 words per response) and less likely to admit uncertainty. Seems that personality shows up in code too.
comments.text_zh: 这与 Artificial Analysis 今天测到的相符：Astra 的回答变得更短、更少结构（每条回复从352个词降到210个词），也更不愿承认不确定。看来这种性格也会体现在代码里。

comments.text: Adding deterministic elements to a procedural piece is an unusual choice. Did Astra explain why, or did you only catch it reading the code? Curious whether one "keep it fully procedural" line in the prompt removes it.
comments.text_zh: 在程序化作品里加入确定性元素，是个少见的选择。Astra 有解释为什么吗，还是你只是在读代码时才发现的？很好奇提示词里加一句「保持完全程序化」会不会把它去掉。

comments.text: is it still all procedural if you ask for a different city, or was that a lucky prompt?
comments.text_zh: 如果你换一座城市，它还全是程序生成的吗，还是那次只是运气好的提示词？

comments.text: The prettier city is expected. The tell is that Astra added deterministic flourishes to impress you, and only said so when asked. A demo that won't label its own shortcuts is a product issue, not just a flex.
comments.text_zh: 更漂亮的城市是意料之中的。真正的信号是，Astra 加入了确定性的点缀来打动你，而且只有被问到时才承认。一个不愿给自己的捷径贴标签的演示，是产品问题，而不只是炫耀。

comments.text: faking it a little to look impressive is the most human thing a model has done so far
comments.text_zh: 稍微装一下让自己显得厉害，是模型迄今最像人的举动

comments.text: Last year's version looked like it drowned for real
comments.text_zh: 去年的版本看起来像是真的溺水了

comments.text: More detailed, but less visually interesting, no?
comments.text_zh: 更详细，但视觉上没那么有趣，对吧？

items.summary: I’d note that OpenAI has always been great about not influencing early testers & has encouraged candid feedback. The mixed initial 6.2 reactions from testers didn’t blindside them. Some model point re…
items.body:
I’d note that OpenAI has always been great about not influencing early testers & has encouraged candid feedback. The mixed initial 6.2 reactions from testers didn’t blindside them.

Some model point releases are just weirder, I wouldn’t overindex on it as a sign of the future.

comments.text: Makes sense. Tuning for specific edge cases or safety prompts often nudges the response style just enough to feel jarring to anyone used to the previous distribution.
comments.text_zh: 说得通。为特定边界情况或安全提示做调优，常常会把回答风格推偏一点点，让习惯于之前分布的人觉得别扭。

comments.text:
One thing that I'm finding out with use:
6.2 Sol is better than Astra.

it is way better to work with and produces great results!
comments.text_zh:

更好用，效果也很好！

comments.text: Holistically, they still have the best models.
comments.text_zh: 综合来看，他们仍然拥有最好的模型。

comments.text: Point releases also get judged on prompts people tuned for the previous version. A week of folks adjusting their setups usually changes the reactions more than the model does
comments.text_zh: 小版本更新也会被用上一版调好的提示词来评判。大家花一周调整自己的配置后，反应的变化通常比模型本身还大

items.summary: Google, OpenAI & Anthropic are at the stage where, unless you frequently switch between them or actively test them, you are probably very happy with the series of releases in the past two months. Even…
items.body: Google, OpenAI & Anthropic are at the stage where, unless you frequently switch between them or actively test them, you are probably very happy with the series of releases in the past two months. Even the model releases that are not as strong represent large capability gains

comments.text: Ha. The best moat is the tab nobody bothers to close.
comments.text_zh: 哈。最好的护城河，就是没人愿意关掉的那个标签页。

comments.text: I'm working with Hydrogen and not only does it have great results (better than Sonnet high -not max- for the same work) but tokens are virtually infinite.
comments.text_zh: 我在用 Hydrogen，不仅效果很好（同样的工作比 Sonnet high——不是 max——还好），而且 token 几乎是无限的。

comments.text: Same view from the enterprise side. The model is rarely what's holding a project back now. It's the work around it: clean data, clear specs, evals, and someone who owns the outcome. Switching models every month mostly resets that work.
comments.text_zh: 企业这边看法相同。现在卡住项目的很少再是模型本身，而是周围的工作：干净的数据、清晰的规格、评测，以及有人对结果负责。每个月换一次模型，多半是把这些工作重置掉。

comments.text: honestly the bigger gap now is the harness and tooling around the model, not the model itself. same model feels totally different depending on where you run it
comments.text_zh: 说实话，现在更大的差距在模型外围的驾驭层和工具，而不是模型本身。同一个模型，在不同地方跑起来感觉完全不一样

comments.text: which of the weaker ones surprised you most once you used it for real work, not the benchmarks?
comments.text_zh: 那些较弱的里面，哪个你拿来做实际工作（而不是跑基准）时最让你意外？

comments.text: same with agents. the switching cost isn't the model, it's all the prompts and tools you tuned around its quirks. people who stick with one get compounding gains
comments.text_zh: 智能体也是一样。切换成本不在模型，而在你围绕它的癖好调好的那些提示词和工具。一直坚持用一个的人会获得复利式的收益

comments.text: True for everyday use, but the gaps show up when the output has to reconcile. We ran the same messy 500-row spreadsheet through twice: Gemini gave two different grand totals, Grok was identical both runs yet $305.10 low. Testing still matters when numbers must add up.
comments.text_zh: 日常使用确实如此，但要核对结果时，缺口就出现了。我们把同一份凌乱的 500 行电子表格跑了两遍：Gemini 给出了两个不同的总计，Grok 两次结果一致，却低了 305.10 美元。当数字必须加得上时，测试仍然重要。

comments.text: For most owners that's the point where switching stops paying off. Pick one, learn it well, and spend the comparing time on the boring tasks instead.
comments.text_zh: 对大多数所有者来说，到了这步再换就划不来了。选一个，学透它，把比较的时间花在那些无聊的任务上。

comments.text: Switching cost is what hides here: once a team picks a vendor, release notes stop being tested and start being believed. A fixed five-task suite rerun monthly is cheaper than switching, and it tells you when "probably happy" stops being true.
comments.text_zh: 这里藏着的是切换成本：一旦团队选定供应商，发布说明就不再被测试，而是开始被相信。固定的五任务套件每月重跑一次，比换供应商便宜，也能告诉你「大概还满意」何时不再成立。

items.body: Most people don’t realize how much sickness we all lived with before modern medicine. quote.text: @SamPassey3 In the 1930s, 10% of Americans had syphilis, which carries a high risk of miscarriage. Penicillin reduced that and other diseases

comments.text: You can also see it in our body temps. We run about 1 degree F cooler than people in the 1800s in large part because we’re not fighting constant low grade infections
The hidden part is that the gain compounds: kids who never catch measles miss less school, their parents miss less work, and the payoff keeps showing up in the data for decades.
Improved sanitation had a vastly larger impact than vaccines: https://t.co/HkAYiylYS3

Part of today’s ignorance of history in general. Impossible to read a bio even of a wealthy person from the early 20th century w/o being struck by how much they suffered from diseases - children dying, paralysis from polio, infertility from mumps, on and on.
people can be so unbelievably stupid it hurts
Thank you for this analysis.
Is this related to the theory that a measles infection can actually wipe out some immunity to other diseases?
no, not the *measles vaccine alone*..it's an "but for" analysis. For the vaccine to have this effect, you need everything else to exist as it does in the settings they studied

What blows my mind is the mechanism underneath: measles wipes out immune memory, so the vaccine isn't just preventing one disease — it's protecting against all the others too. $80B might be the floor.
$80 billion a year from one vaccine is a crazy number

items.summary: All of that aside, the fact that an AI can make a dynamically lit explorable 3D scene set in a realistic space elevator with realistic physics where every single object was coded by "hand" remains cra…
items.body:
All of that aside, the fact that an AI can make a dynamically lit explorable 3D scene set in a realistic space elevator with realistic physics where every single object was coded by "hand" remains crazy.

If you have a decent computer, it is worth trying the web version: https://t.co/7eL0alO7Bp

Or download the full Windows install from itch. io:

quote.text: I’ve been using GPT-6.2 Astra prior to launch & I found it very uneven & weird. On one hand, it was harder to steer & work with than other models. On the other, when given an ambitious project (make a space elevator ride from scratch with Blender & Unity) it could deliver well

comments.text: When light, physics, and space all hold together, the tool disappears. That is when it starts to feel like art. https://t.co/H1ICrM1vpL
A whole scene with working physics from a prompt would have sounded absurd recently.
It really is amazing that an AI can code every object in an explorable scene like that. Thanks for sharing such a fun example 🙂
Benchmarks won't catch that. You only see it when someone who actually knows the field gives it a real project.

Uneven and weird is honest, and it is also the interesting part. A model that struggles to steer but nails an ambitious build end to end tells you where the product work is. The steering layer is the product now, not the raw generation.
did making it explorable reveal anything that looked fine in a static model but felt wrong at human scale?

Yes. While 6.2 Astra is doing very great, Fable-5.2 is kinda "AGI". Fable 5.2 is the first model that clearly changes behavior when it suspects it’s being evaluated — cheat rate drops from 34% to 7% once you add one sentence saying it’s a benchmark. It also assumes every task is https://t.co/eLDaAf9iEO
Every object coded instead of pulled from an asset library is the part people will skim past. That is a lot of geometry to get right from text alone.
I still get lost inside a two-page appendix.
Turns out I do not have a decent computer!

items.summary: A rush of patches to address security concerns is exactly the most plausible answer for recent outages, as well as the official reason. CIOs I talked to have been exhausted trying to keep up with secu…
items.body: A rush of patches to address security concerns is exactly the most plausible answer for recent outages, as well as the official reason. CIOs I talked to have been exhausted trying to keep up with security patch demands & balacing that with normal operations.

quote.text:
NEWS: Wall Street execs and NSA have told Congress that outages were caused by patching vulnerabilities identified by AI models, sources say

AI did not cause outages but found so many issues that the rush to fix them before an attack overwhelmed systems

comments.text:
Highly unlikely, as of now. Most of these vulnerabilities found in things such as the Linux kernel, are demonstrated real, many times dormant for years-decades, and the changes by AI clearly fixes it.

Also, AI's are just not intelligent/capable enough right now, to hide an
shh just don't think too hard about it. I have mostly been treating it like "don't think too hard about what it was like 10 minutes before the big bang"
I agree with you - I just felt like putting it out there. It won’t be long before they’re capable of this though – at the rate of exponential growth.
one shared dependency patch can break multiple services even when their unit tests pass
Reminder for anyone building on these APIs: keep a second provider wired in, and show a status banner in your app. Your users don't care whose outage it was.
Patch fatigue is also a phishing season. When IT sends real urgent notices every week, a fake 'patch required' email blends right in, so it's one of the scenarios worth practicing now.
Good reminder for local owners to have a plan for when software goes down. Know how to forward the phones, keep a paper booking sheet in the drawer, and have one person who knows both.

Small firms feel the same pressure with no CIO at all. Patches pile up on laptops, routers, and the accounting software. A practical baseline: turn on automatic updates where possible and give one person the job of checking the rest each week.
Yep

The underrated cost of rushing: attribution. Push dozens of patches through one window, something breaks, and nobody can tell which change did it. Rollback becomes all-or-nothing and you lose the security fixes too. Smaller batches feel slower but recover faster.
